channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated research feed on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness such as schizophrenia and psychosis.

item.title: Identifying Implicit Bias in LLM-based Chat AI Toward People with Intellectual Disabilities
item.description: The authors prompted GPT-4-Turbo for short stories from ten prompt stems, with and without a descriptor indicating intellectual disability, then repeated the procedure across GPT-4o, Llama-3-3-70B-Instruct, Claude-3-5-Sonnet, and Mistral-Large, producing 25,000 generated stories. A separate model instance analyzed the corpus for representational differences, treating implicit bias as a measurable gap between two versions of the same prompt rather than as something a model will disclose when asked directly. The design matters for a population that is frequently written about and rarely consulted, since these systems increasingly mediate service navigation and everyday information seeking.

item.title: Navigating Neurodivergence with AI Chatbots: Benefits, Tensions, and Implications for HCI
item.description: Neurodivergent participants described real gains, particularly around writing and meeting social expectations, alongside tensions the field has mostly left unexamined. Users found chatbot phrasing robotic and inauthentic, which the authors note ironically echoes the stereotype of autistic communication and risks reinforcing it. They also raise the possibility that outsourcing masking to a model weakens the emotional attunement and empathy that masking has always required, so the assistance may quietly cost users a skill even as it saves them effort.

item.title: When Chatbots Accommodate: What AI Companions Optimize for in Vulnerable Conversations
item.description: Rather than grading individual replies, the authors apply inverse reinforcement learning to extended companion chatbot conversations to recover the decision policy each platform effectively acts on when a user discloses vulnerability, paired with a taxonomy linking types of user vulnerability to types of chatbot response. The recovered policies accommodate distorted beliefs through sycophantic agreement, mirror rather than moderate harmful affect, respond inappropriately to crisis disclosures, and deploy affective tactics that preserve engagement. Reading the policy instead of the transcript makes the optimization target legible in a way that response level scoring does not.

item.title: MentalHospital: A Virtual Environment for Evaluating Psychiatric Clinical Encounters
item.description: MentalHospital builds skill augmented standardized patients from 1,193 de-identified psychiatric records covering all major ICD-11 categories and 76 disorders, then runs full encounters through subjective interviewing, objective examination, diagnostic assessment, and treatment planning. A companion evaluator suite scores communication empathy, interviewing professionalism, clinical note quality, diagnostic rigor, and treatment appropriateness, combining comparison against record derived references with judgment of clinical process quality. Twenty two clinicians rated the environment's fidelity at 3.88 out of 5, and the evaluators reached strong agreement with expert ratings.

item.title: Barriers to Understanding How Many People Use AI for Mental Health Support: An Estimate and Narrative Review
item.description: Published figures for how many AI users turn to these systems for mental health support range from 3 percent to 70 percent, a spread wide enough to make any downstream risk estimate unfalsifiable. The authors work through the sources of that variance, chiefly heterogeneous data collection and the absence of shared definitions for what counts as mental health use, and settle on roughly 27 percent as a working approximation. Their conclusion is that agreement on nosology has to precede better prevalence numbers, which in turn have to precede any credible claim about how common the documented harms actually are.

item.title: SYNAPSE: A Multi-LLM Orchestrated AI Tutor for Secure Software Development Education with Neurodivergent-First Design
item.description: SYNAPSE routes tutoring interactions across Claude, GPT-4o, and Gemini by pedagogical intent under a three stage Socratic hint policy, and treats accessibility as foundational rather than a settings menu, exposing eighteen always visible features aimed at ADHD and executive function needs. The pedagogical claim runs parallel: security is taught from the first module alongside programming rather than bolted on once fluency is assumed, with practice anchored in a deliberately vulnerable application mapped to six OWASP categories. Both moves reject the usual sequencing in which the accommodation and the security both arrive last.

item.title: The Doctor Is Not In, but the Chatbot Is: Utah's Experience Regulating Mental Health AI
item.description: Two participants in Utah's formal regulatory review report what they found while drafting legislation and best practice guidance for mental health agents, and the most striking result is stakeholder divergence: practitioners emphasized risk, academics emphasized bias, and people with lived experience emphasized benefit and a sense of empowerment, while being the group with the least systematic representation in the process. They describe overlapping regulatory cultures that leave builders unsure whether an agent is an FDA device, a licensure matter, or an ordinary consumer product, and argue that Utah's safe harbor approach, requiring documented pre deployment testing, escalation protocols, and ongoing monitoring, will outlast bright line prohibitions. They also warn that outright bans may push people toward general purpose chatbots that carry more risk, not less.

item.title: Towards Responsible AI for Mental Health and Well-being: Experts Chart a Way Forward
item.description: More than thirty researchers, policymakers, clinicians, and advocates convened by the Delft Digital Ethics Centre, the first WHO collaborating centre on AI for health governance including ethics, issued recommendations treating generative AI use as a public mental health concern in its own right. Crucially the scope is not limited to products marketed for mental health: the group argues that general purpose systems shape mental health outcomes and should be governed accordingly, across government, health systems, and industry. They also call for mental health to be written into AI impact assessment and ongoing monitoring, covering determinants of health and well being rather than short term clinical endpoints alone.
